name: Fully Denied Claim
whatHappened: The carrier has denied the claim outright — no payment, no approved scope. This is different from a partial denial or underpayment: the carrier is saying there's nothing to pay for at all.
whatToCheck: The exact reason given in the denial letter (coverage issue vs. no damage found vs. pre-existing/wear and tear)
Whether the denial is about coverage (is this a covered peril at all) or amount (they don't think there's damage)
What documentation exists in the file already
Whether an inspection actually happened and what it found
possibleSolutions: If the denial is based on "no damage found" — request reinspection with new or overlooked documentation
If the denial cites wear and tear, age, or pre-existing damage — gather documentation that distinguishes storm damage from those causes
If the denial is a genuine coverage dispute — this is likely outside what reinspection or appraisal can fix; escalate
If the file is thin — build it out with documentation before pushing back
recommendedFirstMove: Read the denial letter closely and sort it into one of two buckets: a dispute about whether there's covered damage (documentation/reinspection territory) or a dispute about whether it's covered at all (an escalation/coverage question).
whatToSayWrite: To the client: acknowledge the denial, explain in plain terms what it's based on, and let them know you're reviewing next steps — avoid promising an outcome. To the adjuster: ask for the specific basis for the denial in writing if it isn't already clear.
followUp: Within 3-5 business days of receiving the denial
ifUnsuccessful: If the carrier holds the denial after documentation is submitted, evaluate reinspection (if damage-based) or escalate (if coverage-based).
escalationPoint: Any full denial that appears to hinge on a coverage question rather than documentation should go to your lead early — don't spend a week building a documentation case for a dispute documentation can't resolve.

name: Partial Roof Approval
whatHappened: The carrier approved part of the roof (often one slope, or the main structure) but denied or excluded another part — a different slope, a garage, a detached structure, or specific line items.
whatToCheck: Exactly what was approved vs. denied, item by item
The stated reason for excluding the denied portion
Whether the same storm event caused damage to both the approved and denied areas
Whether the denied portion has its own supporting documentation
possibleSolutions: If the excluded area has documented damage that wasn't considered — request reinspection focused specifically on that area
If the carrier's stated reason is material-related (e.g., discontinued shingle, unavailable match) — see the Material Unavailable / Discontinued scenario
If it's a scope/quantity disagreement on the denied portion — push the estimate with a direct comparison
If negotiation stalls — appraisal is often a good fit once the approved portion shows the carrier already accepts the loss
recommendedFirstMove: Isolate the denied portion from the approved portion and treat it as its own mini-case — what's the stated reason, and what evidence would directly answer it?
supportingDocumentation: Full itemized estimate showing approved vs. denied
Photos of the denied area specifically
whatToSayWrite: To the client: explain that part of the claim was approved and part is still being worked, without promising the denied portion will be covered. To the adjuster: ask specifically why the excluded area was treated differently from the approved area.
followUp: 1-2 weeks after submitting additional information on the denied portion
ifUnsuccessful: If the carrier maintains the split after documentation, consider appraisal — the fact that they've already accepted part of the loss often works in your favor.
escalationPoint: Escalate if the carrier's reasoning for the split doesn't hold up on its face (e.g., same storm, same roof, no coherent explanation for the difference).

name: Low Scope / Underpayment
whatHappened: The carrier approved the claim but the scope or dollar amount is lower than what the actual repair requires — missing line items, undercounted quantities, or underpriced work.
whatToCheck: Where exactly your estimate and the carrier's estimate diverge — scope, quantity, or pricing
Whether missing items were simply overlooked or deliberately excluded
Whether quantities were measured correctly
Pricing source the carrier used vs. what's standard locally
possibleSolutions: Push the existing estimate with a clear item-by-item comparison
Request a supplement for specific missing or undercounted items
If it's a broad, unresolved gap — appraisal
Gather manufacturer, code, or measurement documentation to support the disputed items
recommendedFirstMove: Build a side-by-side comparison of your estimate and theirs, and identify which differences are factual (a measurement, a missing item) versus judgment calls (pricing, necessity).
whatToSayWrite: To the adjuster: lead with the factual discrepancies (missing items, wrong quantities) before the judgment calls — those are usually easier to resolve first.
followUp: 1-2 weeks after sending the comparison
ifUnsuccessful: If the carrier won't move on a well-documented comparison, this is a strong appraisal candidate.
escalationPoint: Escalate if the gap is large enough that it materially affects whether the repair can be completed as scoped.

name: Carrier Says Damage Is Wear and Tear
whatHappened: The carrier is denying or limiting the claim on the basis that the damage is normal wear and tear rather than storm-caused, which is typically excluded from coverage.
whatToCheck: What specifically the carrier is pointing to as evidence of wear and tear
Whether there's a clear storm event with a date and documented weather data for the property
Whether the damage pattern is consistent with impact/wind rather than gradual deterioration
The age and condition of the roof prior to the storm, if known
possibleSolutions: Gather storm documentation (weather reports, hail/wind data) tying damage to a specific date
Get an independent assessment distinguishing storm damage from wear patterns
Use photo documentation showing impact-consistent damage (bruising, fractures) vs. gradual wear
If the carrier won't reconsider with solid documentation, this may be appraisal-appropriate since it's a dispute over cause/amount
recommendedFirstMove: Pull storm/weather documentation for the date of loss and pair it with photos that show damage consistent with that event, not gradual wear.
supportingDocumentation: Storm/weather report for the date of loss
whatToSayWrite: To the adjuster: present the storm data and photo evidence together as a single package — don't send it piecemeal. To the client: explain this is a common carrier argument and that you're building the documentation to address it directly.
followUp: 1-2 weeks after submitting storm/damage documentation
ifUnsuccessful: If the carrier maintains the wear-and-tear position after solid documentation, this is a reasonable candidate for appraisal.
escalationPoint: Escalate if the carrier's wear-and-tear argument seems to be a blanket position rather than claim-specific — that pattern is worth flagging to your lead.

name: Carrier Says Damage Is Prior / Pre-Existing
whatHappened: The carrier is attributing the damage to a prior event (an earlier storm, a previous claim, or damage that existed before the policy period) rather than the current claimed loss.
whatToCheck: Whether there's a documented prior claim on this property
The date of the alleged prior damage vs. the current date of loss
Whether the client has records of a prior repair or lack thereof
Any inconsistency in the carrier's timeline
possibleSolutions: Request the carrier's basis for the prior-damage claim in writing (claim number, date, source)
Gather documentation showing the roof's condition before the current date of loss, if available
Interview the client about the property's claim history
If the timeline doesn't hold up, push back directly with the documented current-event evidence
recommendedFirstMove: Ask the carrier to specify exactly what prior event or claim they're referring to — a vague "pre-existing" assertion is much weaker than a documented one, and often falls apart once you ask for specifics.
supportingDocumentation: Storm/weather report for the current date of loss
Any prior inspection or claim records
whatToSayWrite: To the adjuster: ask directly for the specific prior claim or event they're citing, in writing. To the client: ask about any prior roof work or claims on the property so you're not caught off guard.
followUp: 1-2 weeks after requesting specifics from the carrier
ifUnsuccessful: If the carrier won't specify or the claim stalls, this is a reasonable appraisal candidate since it's fundamentally a dispute over cause and amount.
escalationPoint: Escalate if the client discloses a real prior claim that complicates the current one — better to loop in your lead early than be surprised later.

name: Reinspection Request Denied
whatHappened: You requested a reinspection and the carrier refused — either explicitly declining or simply not scheduling one after repeated requests.
whatToCheck: Whether the carrier gave a stated reason for declining
How many times reinspection has been requested and over what timeframe
Whether the original request clearly identified the disputed items and included documentation
Whether the dispute is really about amount rather than needing a fresh look
possibleSolutions: If the request was vague, resubmit with a sharper, better-documented ask
If the carrier has flatly refused, this is a strong signal to move toward appraisal instead
Escalate internally if this is unusual for that carrier or adjuster
recommendedFirstMove: Confirm the original reinspection request was specific and well-documented. If it was, a flat refusal is a strong signal to stop pursuing reinspection and consider appraisal instead — don't keep re-requesting the same thing.
supportingDocumentation: Copy of the original reinspection request
Photos and documentation that were included
whatToSayWrite: To the adjuster: ask them to confirm in writing that reinspection is declined, and why. To the client: let them know reinspection wasn't granted and you're evaluating the next path.
followUp: Immediately after a clear denial — don't let this sit
ifUnsuccessful: Move to appraisal or escalate, depending on claim value and complexity.
escalationPoint: Escalate any flat, unexplained reinspection refusal to your lead — this pattern is worth tracking by carrier.

name: Reinspection Delayed
whatHappened: A reinspection was requested and not explicitly denied, but it's been scheduled and rescheduled, or simply hasn't happened, well past a reasonable timeframe.
whatToCheck: How long it's been since the reinspection was requested or last scheduled
Whether the delay is on the carrier's side, the client's availability, or something else
Whether there's a scheduled date currently on the books
possibleSolutions: Follow up directly with the adjuster for a firm date
If the client's availability is the holdup, work with them to lock in a window
If delays continue without explanation, escalate internally
recommendedFirstMove: Send a direct, dated follow-up asking for a firm reinspection date — vague check-ins tend to get vague answers.
supportingDocumentation: Timeline of requests and any scheduled/rescheduled dates
whatToSayWrite: To the adjuster: ask for a specific date, not just confirmation it's "in the queue." To the client: confirm their availability so scheduling isn't the holdup.
followUp: Every 1-2 weeks until a firm date is set
ifUnsuccessful: If delays continue past a reasonable point (use your judgment based on claim urgency), escalate internally.
escalationPoint: Escalate if a reinspection has been delayed more than once without a clear reason.

name: Adjuster Not Responding
whatHappened: The assigned adjuster has gone quiet — not returning calls or emails — and the claim isn't moving.
whatToCheck: How long it's been since the last response
How many follow-up attempts have been made and through what channels
Whether there's a supervisor or alternate contact on file
Whether the adjuster may have changed (reassignment, leave, turnover)
possibleSolutions: Send one more clear, dated follow-up through the primary channel
Try an alternate channel (phone if you've only emailed, or vice versa)
Contact the carrier's general claims line to check on adjuster status
Escalate to a supervisor if there's still no response after reasonable attempts
recommendedFirstMove: Check your follow-up history first — if you've made 2+ genuine attempts over a reasonable window with no response, it's time to go up a level rather than sending a third similar message.
supportingDocumentation: Log of prior contact attempts and dates
whatToSayWrite: Keep follow-ups short, specific, and dated — state exactly what you need and by when, so a supervisor reading the thread later can see the pattern clearly.
followUp: Every 3-5 business days while unresponsive
ifUnsuccessful: Escalate to the carrier's supervisor line and loop in your own lead.
escalationPoint: Escalate after 2+ unanswered follow-ups over 1-2 weeks, sooner if the claim is time-sensitive.

name: Adjuster Says No Additional Damage
whatHappened: You've identified damage beyond what the carrier approved, but the adjuster maintains there's nothing further to pay for.
whatToCheck: Whether the additional damage was actually inspected or just dismissed verbally
Whether you have clear photo/measurement documentation of the specific additional damage
Whether the adjuster gave any specific reasoning or just a blanket "no"
possibleSolutions: Request reinspection focused specifically on the additional damage, with documentation attached
If reinspection is refused, submit the documentation directly as a reconsideration request
If the carrier still won't budge, this is appraisal territory
recommendedFirstMove: Put together clear, specific documentation of exactly what additional damage exists and where — a vague "there's more damage" claim is easy to dismiss; a marked-up photo set isn't.
supportingDocumentation: Photos of the specific additional damage, clearly marked
whatToSayWrite: To the adjuster: be specific — name the exact areas and items, not a general assertion that more damage exists.
followUp: 1-2 weeks after submitting documentation
ifUnsuccessful: Move to appraisal if the carrier maintains its position after specific, documented evidence.
escalationPoint: Escalate if the adjuster declines to even review documentation you submit.

name: Client Says Insurance "Dropped" the Claim
whatHappened: The client believes the carrier closed or abandoned the claim — this may be accurate (the claim was formally closed) or a misunderstanding (it's just stalled or between steps).
whatToCheck: The claim's actual current status directly with the carrier — don't rely on the client's read of it
Whether there's a formal closure letter or notice
The last actual activity date on the claim
possibleSolutions: If the claim is genuinely closed — determine why and whether it can be reopened
If it's just stalled, reassure and update the client with the real status and next step
If communication broke down, get a direct update from the carrier before saying anything further to the client
recommendedFirstMove: Verify the actual claim status with the carrier before responding to the client — don't confirm or deny what the client believes until you know.
supportingDocumentation: Any closure notice from the carrier
whatToSayWrite: To the client: acknowledge their concern, let them know you're checking the actual status, and follow up with facts rather than reassurance alone.
followUp: Within 2-3 business days of the client raising this
ifUnsuccessful: If the claim was formally closed, escalate internally to determine the best path to reopen or appeal.
escalationPoint: Escalate any formally closed claim to your lead before taking further action.

name: Client Hesitant to Move Forward
whatHappened: The client is dragging their feet on a needed next step — signing something, scheduling access, agreeing to appraisal, or another decision point — often due to confusion, cost concerns, or general uncertainty.
whatToCheck: What specifically the client seems uncertain or concerned about
Whether they fully understand what's being asked of them and why
Whether there's a cost or commitment they're worried about
possibleSolutions: Have a direct conversation to understand the actual hesitation, not just note it as "unresponsive"
Re-explain the next step in plain terms and what happens if it doesn't happen
Address specific concerns (cost, timeline, process) directly rather than repeating the same ask
recommendedFirstMove: Reach out with a plain-language explanation of the next step and ask directly what's giving them pause — hesitation usually has a specific cause that a form follow-up won't surface.
supportingDocumentation: N/A — this is primarily a communication issue
whatToSayWrite: Keep it warm and direct: explain what's needed, why, and what happens if it's delayed — invite questions rather than just re-sending the same request.
followUp: 3-5 business days after the conversation, if no decision yet
ifUnsuccessful: If the client remains unresponsive after a genuine attempt to address their concerns, escalate to your lead or client specialist.
escalationPoint: Escalate if hesitation is blocking a time-sensitive step (like an appraisal deadline).

name: Client Unresponsive
whatHappened: The client isn't answering calls, texts, or emails, and the claim needs their input or action to move forward.
whatToCheck: How long it's been and through how many channels you've tried
Whether there's an alternate contact (spouse, family member, property manager) on file
Whether anything in the file suggests why (they're traveling, dealing with something else, etc.)
possibleSolutions: Try multiple channels (call, text, email) with a clear, specific ask
Reach out to an alternate contact if one exists
Give a clear deadline and consequence in writing if there's a time-sensitive step at risk
recommendedFirstMove: Send one clear, multi-channel outreach that states exactly what's needed and by when, rather than several vague check-ins.
supportingDocumentation: Log of contact attempts and dates
whatToSayWrite: Be direct and specific about what's needed and the timeframe — vague "just checking in" messages are easy to ignore.
followUp: Every 3-5 business days, escalating urgency if time-sensitive
ifUnsuccessful: If unresponsive past a time-sensitive deadline, escalate to your lead for guidance on next steps.
escalationPoint: Escalate if client unresponsiveness threatens to cause a missed deadline (e.g., appraisal demand, reinspection window).

name: Appraisal Demand Delayed
whatHappened: The team has decided appraisal is the right path, but the demand letter hasn't gone out yet — often due to missing information (appraiser selection, documentation) or simply not being prioritized.
whatToCheck: What's actually blocking the demand letter from going out — missing appraiser, missing documentation, or just needs to be done
Whether the client has been informed appraisal is happening
possibleSolutions: Select an appraiser from the roster if that's the holdup
Complete the demand letter template with what's already in the file
Set a specific date to send it rather than leaving it open-ended
recommendedFirstMove: Identify the one specific thing blocking the demand letter and resolve just that — most delays here come down to a single missing piece, not a complicated problem.
whatToSayWrite: To the client, if not already informed: use the appraisal client-explanation template.
followUp: Set a firm send date, not "soon"
ifUnsuccessful: If something outside your control is blocking it (e.g., waiting on client sign-off), escalate for help unblocking it.
escalationPoint: Escalate if the demand letter has been pending more than a week without a clear reason.

name: Appraiser Assigned but Not Responding
whatHappened: Your own selected appraiser isn't responding to updates or requests once appraisal is underway.
whatToCheck: How long it's been since the last response (2-3 weeks is the standard follow-up window)
Whether you've tried multiple contact methods
Whether the appraiser has other claims with your team that might explain a backlog
possibleSolutions: Send a direct follow-up through your usual contact method
Try an alternate contact method if you've only used one
If truly unresponsive over an extended period, loop in your lead about whether a different appraiser should be used going forward
recommendedFirstMove: If it's been under 2-3 weeks, a single clear follow-up is usually enough. If it's been longer, escalate.
whatToSayWrite: Keep the follow-up specific: what you need, and by when.
followUp: 2-3 weeks is the standard check-in window during active appraisal
ifUnsuccessful: Escalate to your lead to discuss options, including appraiser selection going forward.
escalationPoint: Escalate if an appraiser is unresponsive for an extended period with no explanation.

name: Disagreement With Appraiser
whatHappened: During appraisal, your own appraiser and the carrier's appraiser can't agree on the amount of loss — this is a normal part of the process and is exactly what the umpire mechanism exists for.
whatToCheck: Whether the two appraisers have formally reached impasse or are still negotiating
Whether an umpire has been selected
What specifically the disagreement is about
possibleSolutions: Let the appraisers continue trying to reach agreement — this is normal and not itself a problem
If truly at impasse, the umpire process resolves it — confirm this is moving forward
Keep the client informed that this stage can take time without over-explaining the mechanics
recommendedFirstMove: Confirm with your appraiser whether they consider this a genuine impasse requiring an umpire, or still active negotiation.
supportingDocumentation: N/A — this is a process step, not a documentation gap
whatToSayWrite: To the client: this is a normal part of appraisal, not a sign anything has gone wrong.
followUp: Per your standard appraisal follow-up cadence (2-3 weeks)
ifUnsuccessful: If the umpire process itself stalls, escalate to your lead.
escalationPoint: Escalate if the appraisal process itself seems to be breaking down (e.g., no umpire being selected after a reasonable period).

name: Appraisal Award Received
whatHappened: The appraisal process has concluded and an award (the binding amount of loss) has been issued.
whatToCheck: The exact award amount and what it covers
Whether the carrier has acknowledged the award and issued payment information
What's needed for close-out (revised estimate, check details, next steps on any denied/partial portions)
possibleSolutions: Follow up with the carrier on settlement and payment the same day the award is received
Kick off the close-out handoffs — revised estimate, payment tracking, and any next-step confirmation for portions not fully resolved
Update the client with the outcome
recommendedFirstMove: Follow up with the carrier on the settlement letter and payment information the same day — don't let this sit even a day.
whatToSayWrite: To the client: share the outcome clearly and what happens next (payment timing, any remaining steps).
followUp: Same day for the carrier follow-up; then per your close-out process
ifUnsuccessful: If the carrier delays payment after the award, escalate — an award is binding.
escalationPoint: Escalate any delay in carrier follow-through after a binding award — this shouldn't require negotiation.

name: Payment Received but Amount Appears Incorrect
whatHappened: A check or payment has come in, but the amount doesn't match what was approved, awarded, or expected.
whatToCheck: The approved or awarded amount vs. the amount actually received
Whether depreciation was withheld (recoverable depreciation is common and not necessarily an error)
Whether there's a deductible or prior-payment adjustment that explains the difference
Whether this is a partial payment with more expected
possibleSolutions: Compare the payment breakdown line by line against the approval/award
If depreciation was withheld, confirm the process for recovering it once work is complete
If there's a genuine discrepancy with no clear explanation, contact the carrier directly for a breakdown
recommendedFirstMove: Get the itemized payment breakdown from the carrier before assuming there's an error — depreciation holdbacks and deductibles explain most "wrong amount" situations.
whatToSayWrite: To the client: explain any depreciation holdback or deductible clearly so the payment amount makes sense to them.
followUp: Within a few business days of identifying a discrepancy
ifUnsuccessful: If the carrier can't explain the discrepancy, escalate for review.
escalationPoint: Escalate any payment discrepancy that isn't explained by depreciation or deductible.

name: Missing Documentation
whatHappened: The claim file is missing something needed to move forward — could be photos, measurements, a report, or client-provided information.
whatToCheck: Exactly what's missing and why it's needed for the next step
Where it should come from (site visit, client, a report/vendor, existing file)
Whether it's time-sensitive
possibleSolutions: If it requires a site visit — schedule one
If it's client-provided — request it directly with a clear deadline
If it's a report (ITEL, storm data, etc.) — order it from the appropriate source
recommendedFirstMove: Name exactly what's missing and why the next step can't proceed without it — this makes the ask concrete for whoever needs to provide it.
supportingDocumentation: N/A — this scenario is about identifying and closing a documentation gap
whatToSayWrite: Be specific about what's needed and why, whether asking the client, a vendor, or scheduling a visit.
followUp: Based on how time-sensitive the missing item is
ifUnsuccessful: If the documentation can't be obtained, note that clearly in the file and revisit whether the next step needs to change.
escalationPoint: Escalate if the missing documentation is blocking a deadline-driven step (e.g., appraisal demand window).

name: ITEL Required
whatHappened: A material identification/availability report (commonly referred to as ITEL, or similar services like RLS/NTS) is needed to resolve a dispute over whether a matching material is available.
whatToCheck: Whether the shingle or material in question is architectural or 3-tab (see the material decision rule in your Playbooks)
Whether an ITEL-type report has already been ordered for this claim
The carrier's specific stated basis for requiring or disputing material availability
possibleSolutions: Order the appropriate report if one hasn't been obtained yet
If one exists, make sure it was actually submitted to the carrier and acknowledged
Use the report as the core of a documentation-based reconsideration request
recommendedFirstMove: Confirm whether this material dispute actually calls for ITEL under your team's material decision rule before ordering — check the Documentation playbook.
supportingDocumentation: Photos of the material in question
whatToSayWrite: To the adjuster: submit the report with a clear explanation of what it establishes (availability/discontinuation) and why that matters for the claim.
followUp: 1-2 weeks after submitting the report
ifUnsuccessful: If the carrier disputes a clear report finding, this is a solid appraisal candidate.
escalationPoint: Escalate if there's uncertainty about whether ITEL applies to the specific material in question.

name: Material Unavailable / Discontinued
whatHappened: The carrier is treating a damaged area as repairable/matchable, but the specific material (often shingles) is discontinued or unavailable, which usually supports a full-slope or full-roof replacement argument instead of a partial repair.
whatToCheck: Whether material unavailability has actually been documented (ITEL or manufacturer confirmation), or is just assumed
What the carrier's position is based on
Whether this affects one area (e.g., a garage) or a larger portion of the property
possibleSolutions: Establish material unavailability formally through an ITEL-type report or manufacturer documentation
Submit that documentation with a clear explanation connecting unavailability to the need for full replacement of the affected area
Request reconsideration based on the documented unavailability
If the carrier maintains their position after solid documentation, escalate
recommendedFirstMove: Verify and document material availability/discontinuation before doing anything else — this is the fact the whole argument rests on.
whatToSayWrite: To the adjuster: submit the unavailability documentation with a clear, direct explanation — this is a factual question, not a judgment call, so lead with the evidence.
followUp: 1-2 weeks after submitting reconsideration
ifUnsuccessful: If the carrier maintains their position despite documented unavailability, escalate for a decision on next steps.
escalationPoint: Escalate if the carrier disputes clearly documented material unavailability.

name: Matching Issue
whatHappened: There's a dispute over whether replacement materials need to match existing ones (siding, shingles, etc.) closely enough to justify a broader scope of replacement than the carrier approved.
whatToCheck: What specific matching issue is in dispute (color, texture, discontinuation, manufacturer)
Whether any relevant matching-related documentation exists for this situation
How visible the mismatch would be if only the damaged portion were repaired
possibleSolutions: Document the matching issue clearly with photos comparing existing vs. available replacement material
Gather manufacturer information supporting the matching concern
Submit a clear, evidence-based reconsideration request
recommendedFirstMove: Document the matching problem visually and with manufacturer information before submitting anything — a well-illustrated mismatch is far more persuasive than a description of one.
supportingDocumentation: Side-by-side photos of existing vs. available material
whatToSayWrite: To the adjuster: let the photo comparison do the talking — pair it with a short, direct explanation.
followUp: 1-2 weeks after submitting documentation
ifUnsuccessful: If the carrier maintains their position, this is a reasonable appraisal candidate.
escalationPoint: Escalate if you're unsure whether a matching argument applies to a particular material or situation.

name: Code-Related Issue
whatHappened: A local building code requirement affects the scope of repair (e.g., requiring additional work beyond a like-for-like repair), and the carrier's estimate doesn't reflect it.
whatToCheck: The specific code requirement and its source (local building authority, state code)
Whether the carrier's estimate acknowledges code upgrade coverage at all
Whether documentation of the specific code citation exists in the file
possibleSolutions: Gather the specific code documentation/citation that applies
Submit it clearly tied to the specific line items it affects
Confirm whether the policy includes code upgrade coverage, if that's relevant
recommendedFirstMove: Get the specific code citation in writing from the applicable authority before submitting anything — a general "code requires this" claim is much weaker than a citation.
supportingDocumentation: Estimate showing the affected line items
whatToSayWrite: To the adjuster: tie the code citation directly to the specific scope items it affects, rather than a general code argument.
followUp: 1-2 weeks after submission
ifUnsuccessful: If the carrier disputes a documented code requirement, escalate or consider appraisal depending on claim value.
escalationPoint: Escalate if there's any uncertainty about how a code requirement applies to this claim — better to confirm than guess.
